clinicalPearls: Calcium oxalate stones are by far the most common type (~75%), followed by calcium phosphate (~15%), uric acid (~8%), struvite (~1%), and cystine (<1%); many stones are mixtures and contain protein matrix (Harrison 22e p.2448).

Identifying the stone type is clinically important because it informs prognosis and the choice of preventive strategy; patients should be encouraged to retrieve and submit passed stones for composition analysis (Harrison 22e p.2451-2452).

The two classic acute presentations are renal colic and painless gross hematuria; symptom onset reflects a stone moving into the ureter and gives no clue as to when the stone actually formed, since stone growth is typically clinically silent over weeks to years (Harrison 22e p.2450).

Pain radiation depends on stone location: an upper ureteral stone may radiate anteriorly, while a lower ureteral stone may radiate to the ipsilateral testicle (men) or labium (women); a ureterovesical-junction stone can cause urinary urgency and frequency (Harrison 22e p.2450).
Absence of hematuria does not exclude a stone, particularly when urine flow is completely obstructed (Harrison 22e p.2450).

Noncontrast helical CT is the gold-standard imaging test: it detects stones as small as 1 mm and visualizes uric acid stones that are traditionally considered radiolucent on plain films (Harrison 22e p.2450).

Urine pH governs solubility of several stone types: uric acid stones form at pH consistently <=5.5, calcium phosphate stones are favored at pH >=6.5, and cystine is more soluble at higher pH; calcium oxalate stone risk is not influenced by urine pH (Harrison 22e p.2450).

Urine citrate is the most clinically important natural inhibitor of calcium-containing stones; metabolic acidosis (including from high animal-flesh intake) lowers citrate excretion by enhancing its tubular reabsorption (Harrison 22e p.2448, 2449).

Dietary calcium restriction is counterproductive: higher dietary calcium intake lowers stone risk by binding intestinal oxalate and reducing urinary oxalate, whereas low calcium intake increases stone risk and may lower bone density (Harrison 22e p.2449).

Two 24-h urine collections on the patient's usual diet are the cornerstone of preventive evaluation, measuring volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, pH, and creatinine; two collections are needed because of substantial day-to-day variability (Harrison 22e p.2451-2452).

Urinary risk factors (calcium, oxalate, citrate) are continuous variables with no valid normal/abnormal cutoff; dichotomizing them is misleading and arbitrary thresholds should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.2449, 2452).
Pure uric acid stones can be recognized by their low Hounsfield units on CT, helping distinguish stone composition non-invasively (Harrison 22e p.2452).
harrison.pathophysiology: Stones form when urine becomes supersaturated with lithogenic solutes, i.e., when the concentration product exceeds the solubility product. Most people's urine is supersaturated for one or more crystal types, but crystallization inhibitors (notably urine citrate) prevent continuous stone formation. Recent biopsy data have shifted the paradigm for stone initiation: calcium phosphate deposits in the renal interstitium, hypothesized to begin at the thin limb of the loop of Henle, then extends to and erodes through the papillary epithelium, forming Randall's plaque on which most calcium oxalate stones grow. Tubular plugs of calcium phosphate may initiate calcium phosphate stones. Thus stone formation can begin years before a stone is clinically detectable. Higher urine calcium (from greater GI absorption and/or bone turnover) and higher urine oxalate (largely dietary, with higher dietary calcium reducing GI oxalate absorption) raise calcium oxalate/phosphate risk, while low urine citrate removes a key inhibitor (Harrison 22e p.2448-2450).
additionalDifferentials: Acute appendicitis (stone at right pelvic brim)
Acute diverticulitis (stone at left pelvic brim)
Acute pyelonephritis (obstructing stone with proximal infection)
Ureteral obstruction by blood clot or sloughed papilla
Extraluminal ureteral compression (typically gradual onset, not true colic)
infectionMimics: Acute pyelonephritis (an obstructing stone with proximal infection can present this way)
Bacterial cystitis (ureterovesical stone causes urgency/frequency with red and white cells in urine but a negative urine culture)
additionalInvestigations: Noncontrast helical CT (gold standard; detects stones as small as 1 mm and uric acid stones)
Renal ultrasound (avoids radiation, shows hydronephrosis, but insensitive for ureteral stones)
Plain abdominal radiograph (KUB) (may miss ureteral/renal stones and gives no obstruction information)
Urinalysis with sediment examination for red/white cells and crystals (calcium oxalate dihydrate = bipyramidal; cystine = hexagonal)
Urine culture if infection is suspected
Serum electrolytes (for hypokalemia/RTA), creatinine, calcium, phosphorus, uric acid
PTH and 25-hydroxy vitamin D when serum/urine calcium is elevated or high/low-normal
At least two 24-h urine collections on usual diet (volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, pH, creatinine; supersaturation when available)
Stone composition analysis of any passed or retrieved stone
redFlags: UTI in the setting of an obstructing stone is a urologic emergency ('pus under pressure') requiring urgent restoration of drainage via ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy
Complete urinary obstruction by a stone (hematuria may be absent)
Stone measuring >=6 mm or anatomic abnormality (low probability of spontaneous passage)
Staghorn or multiple bilateral stones (suggest cystinuria or struvite/infection stones)
Infection (struvite) stones, which if untreated can lead to end-stage renal disease
harrison.prognosis: Although renal colic is reported as among the worst pain patients experience, nephrolithiasis is rarely fatal. More than half of first-time stone formers have a recurrence within 10 years, but recurrence of most or all stone types can be prevented with careful evaluation and targeted, often lifelong, intervention. Untreated infection (struvite) stones can have devastating consequences and progress to end-stage renal disease, and repeated obstruction and instrumentation (e.g., in cystinuria) can reduce GFR. Primary hyperoxaluria can cause intraparenchymal calcium oxalate deposition leading to renal failure (Harrison 22e p.2448, 2450, 2451).
pitfalls: Assuming a normal urinalysis (no hematuria) rules out a stone, which is false especially with complete obstruction
Recommending low dietary calcium, which actually increases stone risk and harms bone density
Using arbitrary normal/abnormal thresholds for urine calcium, oxalate, or citrate when risk is continuous
Basing the preventive regimen on a single 24-h urine collection despite large day-to-day variability
Mistaking a preexisting residual stone for a new stone when baseline imaging was suboptimal, leading to unnecessary changes in therapy
Misattributing flank/abdominal pain to a stone and missing cholecystitis, appendicitis, diverticulitis, AAA, or an occlusive vascular event
Failing to recognize that symptom onset does not indicate when the stone formed
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading; clinical risk stratification rests on likelihood of spontaneous passage (stone size and location, e.g., >=6 mm or anatomic abnormality favoring intervention) and on presence of emergency features such as obstruction with superimposed infection.
management: Manage acute renal colic with analgesia (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, with opioids if needed) and antiemetics, offering medical expulsive therapy with an alpha-blocker to aid passage of a ureteric stone
Urgently decompress an obstructed, infected kidney with a ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy alongside antimicrobial therapy, as this is a urological emergency
Remove stones that will not pass by ureteroscopy, extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy according to stone size, site and composition
Encourage high fluid intake to maintain dilute urine, with dietary measures of reduced sodium, moderate animal protein and adequate dietary calcium

Analyse the passed stone and undertake metabolic evaluation to target prevention, using a thiazide diuretic and potassium citrate for recurrent calcium stones and urinary alkalinisation with potassium citrate for uric acid stones
Use a xanthine oxidase inhibitor (allopurinol) for hyperuricosuric stone formers, and hydration with alkalinisation plus a thiol-binding agent (tiopronin or penicillamine) for cystine stones
Ensure complete stone clearance and treat the underlying infection for struvite (infection) stones
Provide follow-up imaging and biochemical monitoring to detect recurrence and guide lifelong prevention
